Gemcitabine alone: nasopharyngeal cancerNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00514

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.
Record actual treatment dates and dose changes. Your clinician confirms the course length and any later phase.
· copy this sheet for another cycle of the same phase.
□ Tiredness improves with rest
□ Rest does not help; usual tasks affected: call
□ Self-care difficult: urgent review
□ New small bruise / brief bleed: report
□ Repeated bleeding: call today
□ Bleeding that will not stop: urgent help
□ Heavy bleeding / collapse: 112/999
□ Queasy but eating and drinking
□ Intake reduced: contact the team
□ Unable to maintain intake: urgent review
□ Collapse / severe dehydration: 112/999

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, persistent vomiting or inability to drink needs urgent oncology advice. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Gemcitabine is used to control the cancer and relieve symptoms. Your team discusses expected benefit, alternatives and when to review whether treatment is helping.
Gemcitabine is converted inside cells into forms that disrupt DNA building blocks and DNA copying. It can affect normal blood-cell production as well as cancer cells.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bruising, breathlessness, swelling or reduced urine urgently. Flu-like symptoms cannot safely be assumed to be a harmless drug effect.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

The team reviews symptoms, side effects and response. Treatment may finish earlier if it is no longer helping or causes unacceptable problems.

Checks infection-fighting cells, oxygen-carrying cells and platelets for clotting.

Gemcitabine is given into a vein over 30 minutes on Days 1 and 8. Checks, preparation and observation add to the time in the unit. Report new symptoms before dosing.

Follow prescribed support medicines. Blood counts and side effects may change between visits; this is not a guaranteed safe period. Call the team promptly if unwell. Keep the Day-8 blood-test and treatment appointment.
Full blood count before each treatment; kidney and liver blood tests before each cycle. Day-8 decisions use their own blood-count and toxicity rules.
Keep the next test and treatment dates. Fatigue and low blood counts may occur between visits. Do not wait for the next visit if unwell.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
Confirm the next tests, medicines, treatment dates and verified daytime and out-of-hours contact numbers.
Ask about transport, work, costs, communication needs and whether a support person can attend.
Use the prescribed medicines for the active treatment day. The regimen is classified as low sickness risk.
Follow your unit’s oral-care plan. Tell the team early about mouth pain, weight loss, choking or difficulty eating and drinking. Dietetic and swallowing support can help.

Fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, persistent vomiting or inability to drink needs urgent oncology advice. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112/999.
Bring prescription, non-prescription and herbal medicines. Check interactions, allergies and any changes with the oncology pharmacist.
Ask about fatigue, work, transport, caring responsibilities, emotional support and help with appointments.

Your team explains cancer-specific tests, including Epstein–Barr virus tests where relevant in nasopharyngeal cancer. These are distinct from blood tests used for medicine safety. No universal tumour-marker schedule is prescribed here.
Discuss expected benefit, possible lasting effects, suitable alternatives and the option of declining treatment. Tell the team what matters most to you.
Keep a record of symptoms and medicines taken. Do not wait for a routine appointment when symptoms are worsening.
Tell the team about pain, dry mouth, taste changes, choking, reduced intake or weight loss. Ask for a personalised oral-care, dietetic and swallowing plan.

If you are having head and neck radiation, follow the radiation team’s dental, skin, saliva and swallowing advice during and after treatment. Radiation appointments and late-effect checks have their own plan.
Pace activity according to symptoms. Ask for help with fatigue, sleep, work, travel or caring responsibilities.
Discuss fertility preservation before treatment where appropriate. Ask about contraception, pregnancy, breastfeeding and medicine-specific timeframes.
Report pain, redness, swelling, leaking or a wet dressing. Do not adjust infusion equipment yourself; contact the unit.

The medicines act together to shrink or control nasopharyngeal cancer. Your team records how this course fits any planned radiation treatment and your overall treatment aim.
Gemcitabine is converted inside cells into forms that disrupt DNA building blocks and DNA copying. It can affect normal blood-cell production as well as cancer cells.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bruising, breathlessness, swelling or reduced urine urgently. Flu-like symptoms cannot safely be assumed to be a harmless drug effect.

Cisplatin links strands of DNA, the instructions inside cells, making it harder for cancer cells to repair damage and divide. Healthy cells may also be affected. Kidney function, hearing, blood counts and nerve symptoms help the team decide whether the next dose is safe.
What to watch forReport reduced urine, persistent vomiting, tinnitus, hearing change or new tingling.

Chemotherapy is given with radiation to improve control of cancer in the head and neck. Your team confirms that this particular four-day carboplatin schedule suits your cancer and health.

Carboplatin interferes with DNA repair and cell division. Its dose is calculated from kidney function. Blood counts can fall, including platelets that help stop bleeding. It is a different prescription from cisplatin. AUC is a prescribing target for drug exposure, not the number of milligrams in your bag; your clinical team calculates the dose using kidney function.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, marked tiredness or an infusion reaction.

Fluorouracil, often shortened to 5-FU, interferes with the building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, which cells need to grow. It runs through a vein over the prescribed hours. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is an enzyme that breaks it down. Testing for DPD deficiency before treatment reduces risk but cannot rule out every severe reaction.
What to watch forReport severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.

From preparing the line to coming home after disconnection. Your team arranges the appointments and shows you what to do.
A trained professional checks the infusion, disconnects the pump and cares for the line. The appointment is based on connection time.
A port needle can be removed while the port stays under the skin. A peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) remains in the arm with ongoing dressing and line care.

A port is a small chamber beneath the skin, usually on the chest, attached to a tube ending in a large vein. A special needle goes through the skin into the port when it is used. A PICC enters a vein in the upper arm; a short section remains outside under a dressing. Both can deliver a home infusion. Your team helps choose the device and teaches its care.

Tell the team about allergies, blood thinners, infections and any other cancer medicines. Follow the instructions about eating, drinking and transport; do not stop medicines yourself. Port placement uses local anaesthetic, sometimes with sedation or general anaesthetic. The team explains the procedure and risks, including infection, bleeding, clots and insertion complications. Ask how to manage discomfort, protect the wound and resume activity. Report increasing pain, redness, swelling, discharge or fever.

The nurse checks the line and treatment, secures the connection and dressing, and starts the pump. Before leaving, you should have the disconnection location and time, contact numbers including out of hours, and the written spill instructions. Ask to be shown what normal pump progress looks like. You do not need to calculate a rate.

Use the supplied carrier and the position recommended for your pump. Keep tubing free from pulling and kinks. Ask how to place the pump safely for sleep and how to protect the line and dressing when washing. Do not immerse it or swim. Avoid direct heat and cold. An elastomeric pump has a balloon that shrinks slowly and may have no alarm; an electronic pump has different instructions. Follow the instructions for the device you actually receive.

Keep the appointment even if the pump looks empty, unless the team changes the plan. Staff check the pump and line and arrange safe disposal. After flushing and other line care as required, the port needle may be removed and a small dressing applied. The implanted port stays in place until a separate removal procedure is arranged. A PICC remains in place and needs scheduled dressing and flushing care.

Call the team immediately if the pump leaks, is damaged, finishes unexpectedly early, appears not to run, or the line disconnects. Follow the emergency or spill steps you have been specifically taught, including use of a clamp if instructed. Do not reconnect, change settings or disconnect the pump yourself. Keep other people away from leaked medicine. If medicine touches skin, rinse it off and wash with soap and water, then seek advice.

Contact oncology immediately for pain or swelling around the line, a wet/loose dressing, redness, fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell. A painful swollen arm or neck needs urgent advice. Severe chest pain, major breathing difficulty or collapse: call 112 / 999. Do not wait for pump disconnection or the next clinic visit.

Follow your unit’s oral-care plan. Tell the team early about mouth pain, weight loss, choking or difficulty eating and drinking. Dietetic and swallowing support can help.

Chemotherapy is given with radiation to improve control of cancer in the head and neck. Your team confirms the treatment aim and why carboplatin is suitable for your circumstances.

Carboplatin interferes with DNA repair and cell division. Its dose is calculated from kidney function. Blood counts can fall, including platelets that help stop bleeding. It is a different prescription from cisplatin. AUC is a prescribing target for drug exposure, not the number of milligrams in your bag; your clinical team calculates the dose using kidney function.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, marked tiredness or an infusion reaction.

Fluorouracil, often shortened to 5-FU, interferes with the building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, which cells need to grow. It runs through a vein over the prescribed hours. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is an enzyme that breaks it down. Testing for DPD deficiency before treatment reduces risk but cannot rule out every severe reaction.
What to watch forReport severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.

From preparing the line to coming home after disconnection. Your team arranges the appointments and shows you what to do.
A trained professional checks the infusion, disconnects the pump and cares for the line. The appointment is based on connection time.
A port needle can be removed while the port stays under the skin. A peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) remains in the arm with ongoing dressing and line care.

A port is a small chamber beneath the skin, usually on the chest, attached to a tube ending in a large vein. A special needle goes through the skin into the port when it is used. A PICC enters a vein in the upper arm; a short section remains outside under a dressing. Both can deliver a home infusion. Your team helps choose the device and teaches its care.

Tell the team about allergies, blood thinners, infections and any other cancer medicines. Follow the instructions about eating, drinking and transport; do not stop medicines yourself. Port placement uses local anaesthetic, sometimes with sedation or general anaesthetic. The team explains the procedure and risks, including infection, bleeding, clots and insertion complications. Ask how to manage discomfort, protect the wound and resume activity. Report increasing pain, redness, swelling, discharge or fever.

The nurse checks the line and treatment, secures the connection and dressing, and starts the pump. Before leaving, you should have the disconnection location and time, contact numbers including out of hours, and the written spill instructions. Ask to be shown what normal pump progress looks like. You do not need to calculate a rate.

Use the supplied carrier and the position recommended for your pump. Keep tubing free from pulling and kinks. Ask how to place the pump safely for sleep and how to protect the line and dressing when washing. Do not immerse it or swim. Avoid direct heat and cold. An elastomeric pump has a balloon that shrinks slowly and may have no alarm; an electronic pump has different instructions. Follow the instructions for the device you actually receive.

Keep the appointment even if the pump looks empty, unless the team changes the plan. Staff check the pump and line and arrange safe disposal. After flushing and other line care as required, the port needle may be removed and a small dressing applied. The implanted port stays in place until a separate removal procedure is arranged. A PICC remains in place and needs scheduled dressing and flushing care.

Call the team immediately if the pump leaks, is damaged, finishes unexpectedly early, appears not to run, or the line disconnects. Follow the emergency or spill steps you have been specifically taught, including use of a clamp if instructed. Do not reconnect, change settings or disconnect the pump yourself. Keep other people away from leaked medicine. If medicine touches skin, rinse it off and wash with soap and water, then seek advice.

Contact oncology immediately for pain or swelling around the line, a wet/loose dressing, redness, fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell. A painful swollen arm or neck needs urgent advice. Severe chest pain, major breathing difficulty or collapse: call 112 / 999. Do not wait for pump disconnection or the next clinic visit.

Gemcitabine is converted inside cells into forms that disrupt DNA building blocks and DNA copying. It can affect normal blood-cell production as well as cancer cells.

A randomised study of 480 patients compared this three-cycle induction approach followed by chemoradiotherapy with chemoradiotherapy alone. At three years, 85.3% versus 76.5% were alive without recurrence. Severe acute side effects were more frequent with induction (75.7% versus 55.7%). These group results do not predict your personal outcome.
